items.q: The science of eloquent Arabic, fitting speech to its situation.
The three branches of balagha.
A comparison of one thing with another, like "he is like a lion".
A comparison with the "like" word and one side dropped, "a lion spoke".
Saying one thing but meaning something linked to it, like "long of sword-belt" for tall.
Words that sound alike but differ in meaning.
Putting opposites together, like day and night.
Rhyming endings in prose.
The four parts of a tashbih include the two things compared, the tool and this.
The thing compared in a tashbih.
The thing it is compared to.
"Like" (ka-) and "mithl" are examples of this.
The branch of balagha about beautifying speech.
The branch about expressing one meaning in different clear ways.
The branch about fitting the sentence to the situation.
A sentence that can be true or false.
A sentence that cannot be true or false, like a command or question.
Speaking briefly with full meaning.
Speaking at length for a purpose.
The modern school textbook of balagha by 'Ali al-Jarim and Mustafa Amin.
A tashbih with both the tool and the shared quality dropped, the strongest kind.
A tashbih that compares a whole picture with a whole picture.
A metaphor that names the thing compared to, dropping the thing compared.
A metaphor that drops the thing compared to, keeping one of its features.
Using a word for something related, like "hand" for favour.
Using a word in its first meaning.
Using a word outside its first meaning, with a link.
Putting a part for the whole, like "eye" for a spy.
Speaking of the place for its people, like "the village asked".
Words alike in letters, order and vowels, but different meanings.
Words alike but not fully, differing in one feature.
Putting two meanings side by side and then their opposites in order.
Giving a reason for something that is not its real reason, in a beautiful way.
Saying something with two meanings, a near and a far, and meaning the far one.
Praise that sounds like blame.
Putting a word first that usually comes later, to show focus.
Limiting, as in "innama" or "ma ... illa".
Leaving words out because they are understood.
Joining sentences with "wa".
Leaving sentences unjoined.
The book of 'Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani رحمة الله عليه on 'ilm al-bayan and imagery.
The book of 'Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani رحمة الله عليه on 'ilm al-ma'ani and word order.
'Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani's theory of meaning through word order.
The summary of Miftah al-'Ulum by al-Khatib al-Qazwini رحمة الله عليه.
The long commentary of al-Taftazani رحمة الله عليه on al-Talkhis.
The shorter commentary of al-Taftazani رحمة الله عليه on al-Talkhis.
The poem on balagha by al-Akhdari رحمة الله عليه.
The widely taught book of balagha by Hifni Nasif and others.
The early writer of al-Bayan wal-Tabyin.
The caliph's son and poet who wrote Kitab al-Badi', one of the first books of badi'.
The number of kinds of badi' Ibn al-Mu'tazz listed as the main ones.
Asking a question not to learn but to show surprise or denial.
A command that is not really a command, but a request from a lower to a higher.
A command from equal to equal.
A command that means "do it if you can".
A switch in the person spoken of, like from "He" to "You".
Surah al-Fatihah shows iltifat when it turns from "Him" to this.
Repeating a word or idea to stress it.
The figure in which the speaker ends with a line that fits its start.
A line of verse containing a word that also points to a Qur'anic verse or hadith, used respectfully.
Borrowing a line of another poet into one's own poem.
Starting a speech or poem with something that hints at its subject.
Moving smoothly from the opening to the main subject.
Ending in a way that feels complete.
A sentence that reads the same backwards, letter by letter.
Describing something beyond what is possible, as a figure of speech.
The khabar told to a doubter needs this.
The khabar told to one who denies needs this.
items.a: More than one tool of emphasis

items.q: The khabar told to one with no idea at all, needing no emphasis, is called this.
The kind of khabar for a doubter.
The kind of khabar for a denier.
"Musawah" means this kind of speech.
A metaphor carried on with features of the thing compared to.
A metaphor carried on with features of the thing compared.
A metaphor that compares a whole saying with a whole state, like a proverb.
The scholar whose al-Idah expanded al-Talkhis.
Al-Qazwini رحمة الله عليه was the chief judge of this city.
The term for speech that fits its situation, the root of balagha.
The Ash'ari Qadi who wrote I'jaz al-Qur'an.
The poem by al-Suyuti رحمة الله عليه that puts al-Talkhis into verse.
The book by al-'Askari on the two arts of poetry and prose.
The kind of jinas where one side is made of two words joined.
The kind of jinas where the words differ in the order of letters.
The kind of jinas where the words differ in dots only.
A tashbih where the comparison is hidden, not stated.
A tashbih that is reversed, making the weaker the model.
The figure of listing items and then their matches in order.
The figure of listing items and then their matches out of order.
The figure of gathering several things under one ruling.
The figure of separating things that share a ruling.
A metaphor whose base word is a verb or particle, not a noun.
A metaphor whose base word is a noun.
The link that allows a majaz is called this.
The clue that shows a word is not meant literally.
A majaz of attribution, as in "the day fasted" (meaning the person fasted).
A kinayah for a quality, like "her earrings are far" for a long neck.
Al-Akhdari رحمة الله عليه, author of al-Jawhar al-Maknun and al-Sullam, lived in this land.
'Abd al-Qahir al-Jurjani رحمة الله عليه died in this year.
The book of al-Sakkaki whose third part set out balagha in its classic form.
items.src: Miftah al-'Ulum; check al-Sakkaki's creed before adding an honorific

items.q: The book of al-Rummani on the i'jaz of the Qur'an, one of the early three treatises.
items.src: Thalath Rasa'il fi I'jaz al-Qur'an; to be checked
